title: Shemot: why hast thou dealt ill? (Exodus 5:22–6:1)
hook: when things get worse, Moses complains to God, and God answers him

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: a doubting Moses, and God's question, what is that in thy hand? The staff in your hand. Today Moses finally goes to Pharaoh, and it goes badly.

You did the brave thing. You spoke up at work, set the boundary, finally made the call. And things got worse. The boss is colder, the family angrier, and the people you were trying to help now blame you. Moses has just done exactly what God told him. He walked into Pharaoh's palace and said, let my people go. Pharaoh's answer: who is this God? And from now on, no more straw for the bricks. Find your own, and make the same number. The Israelite foremen are beaten. And they turn on Moses.
screen: `YOU DID THE BRAVE THING.` → `AND IT GOT WORSE.` → `NO MORE STRAW.`

segments.voice: So Moses goes back to God, and he doesn't use polite words. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "Lord, wherefore hast Thou dealt ill with this people? why is it that Thou hast sent me?" In Hebrew, lamah hare'otah: why have you done harm? Since I came to Pharaoh in your name, he goes on, it's gotten worse, and you haven't saved them at all. That's a man shouting at heaven, and the Torah keeps it in. Then God answers, not with punishment, but with: "Now shalt thou see what I will do to Pharaoh." This isn't a one-off. Jewish scripture is full of people arguing with God. Abraham, bargaining over Sodom, asks: shall not the Judge of all the earth do justly? Job curses the day he was born. Psalm after psalm asks God, how long? And in a later Hasidic story, Rabbi Levi Yitzchak of Berditchev, tradition says, put God on trial on behalf of his suffering people. In fairness to the other side, Rashi, reading the next verses, hears a rebuke: the patriarchs were promised much and never questioned God like this. So even the commentators argue about the arguing. But the text itself is clear: Moses can say it. The complaint doesn't end the relationship. It's part of it. You only argue this hard with someone you expect to answer.
screen: `LAMAH HARE'OTAH — WHY HARM THEM?` · `NOW SHALT THOU SEE.` · `ABRAHAM, JOB, THE PSALMS.` · `RASHI HEARS A REBUKE.` · then, large: `YOU CAN SAY IT.`

segments.voice: Think of something that's gotten worse even though you tried to do right, and say it plainly in your head, without tidying it up: this isn't fair, and here's why. If you pray, say it to God the way Moses did, in your own blunt words; if you don't, say it to the quiet. Then just sit, and listen for whatever comes back.
Shemot. The portion that ends with Moses demanding, why hast thou dealt ill with this people, and God answering: now you'll see.
Your line: you can say it. Even Moses shouted at heaven, and heaven answered. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Protest and lament are part of Jewish prayer: the Psalms and the Book of Job are full of complaint, and Jewish tradition makes room for speaking to God bluntly, in one's own words, as well as in the fixed prayers.
